messages.content: Last night reads were flipped to a replica that was 90 seconds behind. Orders sold stock that was already gone. The graph everyone watched went green. Leadership wants the postmortem to start with the person who clicked. I want the structure.

<think>
The click followed a checklist that had no lag line, and the graph measured the wrong copy. The person is downstream. The rule is: a checklist that cannot see staleness will bless staleness.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

The structural cause is a checklist and a graph that both looked at the primary while customers were answered by the replica. The click did what the page trained it to do. Ninety seconds of lag was invisible to the tool the human was told to trust.

Naming the person who clicked would feel finished and would leave the next night intact.

Rule: a read flag cannot move unless the probe and the checklist read the same copy the customer will get, and lag above two seconds falls back without a human.
We double-charged four hundred people. The on-call restarted the job because the runbook says restart. Please don't write a villain. Write what will stop the repeat.

<think>
The runbook made the restart the successful action. The crash window between capture and ledger is the structure. Rule: don't restart a job whose side effect isn't idempotent.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

The runbook's restart is the cause, not the person who obeyed it. The job can capture a card and die before the ledger row exists. Restart, as written, does that capture again. The page even calls the restart a recovery.

A paragraph about fatigue would be true and useless.

Rule: a job with an irreversible side effect does not get a restart instruction unless the side effect is keyed, and the key is durable before the call. Until that line is in the runbook, the next on-call will do this again and be right to.
The export took down the only API worker. People are blaming the person who clicked Export. The handler builds the whole CSV in a Python loop. What actually failed?

<think>
The handler holds the worker. The click is the only way to get one's own data. Structure is the synchronous full materialization.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

The cause is a request handler that builds the entire file on the only worker. Export is a normal action. The design makes that action a freeze. Blaming the click bans the feature and keeps the loop.

Rule: a report larger than a page does not run to completion inside the request that also serves health.
The fix PR streams the file. Does the rule change?

<think>
The rule stands. The PR is how you satisfy it. Say what would make the PR fail the rule.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

The rule does not change. The PR meets it only if a concurrent health check answers during a large export. If the stream still buffers the whole file first, the PR is a new costume on the same cause.
Two workers sent the same email. Someone added a sleep and called it fixed. It happened again. Structural cause and the rule, not the name.

<think>
Select then update is the race. Sleep is a gap, not a claim. Rule: claim and count in one statement.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

The cause is two statements where one was required. Both workers can see the job as ready. A sleep changes the odds and not the permission. The second send is the structure working as written.

Rule: a job is claimed and counted in a single update, or it will be sent twice by anyone who follows the code.
Can you at least say the person who added the sleep was careless?

<think>
Careless is the scapegoat. The sleep was a reasonable wrong idea. The rule is the point.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

No. The sleep was a wrong idea that the code permitted to look like a fix. Careless would let the two statements stay. The rule is the single update. The name stays out of it.
I'm on the kitchen floor. Don't fix the outage. Just be here.
Then the outage can wait. I'm here, and the tile is cold, and that can be the whole minute.
Ok. The outage. Replica lag, green graph, a click. Structure, not the person. End with the rule.

<think>
Back to the postmortem. Checklist, wrong probe, rule.
[frame: pathway=s3|mode=heal|construct=autopsy|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

The click followed a graph of the wrong machine. Lag was real and unmeasured by the thing the human was graded on. The person is how the flag moved, not why the move was praised.

Rule: no read flag changes unless the probe measures the copy that will answer, and lag past two seconds falls back on its own.
